Learning Who Talks to Whom: Role-Aware Communication Topology Scheduling for Efficient LLM Multi-Agent Collaboration

Haibin Li Affiliation: Beihang University    Wenya Yu Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University    Xuefeng Jiang Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences    Jia Li Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences    Xiao Han Affiliation: Beihang University    Shuai Su Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University    Wei Wei Affiliation: Beihang University
Abstract

Multi-agent systems driven by large language models (LLMs) rely on structured communication topologies to facilitate information exchange and collaborative reasoning. However, effectively scheduling these topologies to dynamically determine who talks to whom and when to communicate remains a fundamental challenge in balancing collective reasoning performance against exponential token overhead. Existing topology scheduling approaches either enforce static communication graphs that cannot adapt to dynamic problem-solving states, or overlook agent role complementarity while failing to explicitly incorporate the synthesized graph structure into team-level decision evaluation. To tackle these limitations, we propose ACTS, a role-aware adaptive communication topology scheduling framework for efficient LLM multi-agent collaboration. Orchestrated within a Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm, ACTS introduces a novel dual-attention mechanism. Specifically, a Role-conditioned Relational Attention module dynamically selects variable-cardinality interaction partners based on agent roles and evolving execution states, while a Topological Attention Mixer explicitly embeds the directed communication topology into team value decomposition for precise credit assignment. Comprehensive evaluations across 9 challenging benchmarks covering code generation, multi-step reasoning, general knowledge, and competitive mathematics demonstrate that ACTS consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, boosting average accuracy by up to 6.19 percentage points while reducing token consumption by over 15%. The project website is available at https://acts-mas.github.io/ACTS/.

††footnotetext: * Equal contribution; †\dagger Corresponding authors.

1 Introduction

LLM-based multi-agent systems combine heterogeneous roles and complementary reasoning perspectives to solve complex tasks (Du et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023). Structured communication supports evidence sharing and cross-agent verification but increases token consumption and inference latency (Yan et al., 2025). Exchanges that overlook agent contributions or evolving execution states may introduce redundant information (Liu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025). This motivates role-aware adaptive topology scheduling to determine when and between which agents communication occurs, balancing task performance against communication cost (Zhang et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2026).

Existing communication-topology scheduling methods can be classified into static approaches, task-adaptive approaches, and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL)-based approaches. Static methods retain predefined interaction structures across tasks and communication rounds (Du et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023). Task-adaptive methods generate task-specific graphs through topology induction or architecture search (Zhang et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2026), but commonly determine the complete topology before execution. Their directed links consequently remain fixed during interaction and cannot adapt to evolving local states. MARL-based topology-scheduling methods make communication decisions during execution. Agent Q-Mix(Jiang et al., 2026) is a representative MARL-based topology-scheduling method that constructs directed topologies from selected communication modes through predefined rules. Under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), a QMIX (Rashid et al., 2018) monotonic mixing network combines individual utilities using global information during training, and agents select actions from local observations during execution. However, its partner selection is not explicitly conditioned on agent roles or evolving execution states, and its mixer does not encode the realized directed incoming and outgoing neighborhoods of individual agents. These limitations constrain adaptive partner selection and topology-specific credit assignment.

To address these limitations, this work proposes ACTS, a role-aware framework for Adaptive Communication Topology Scheduling under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE). Each agent uses a local action-value function to decide when and how to communicate. Role-aware relational attention selects variable-cardinality directed partner sets from role embeddings and evolving local states, determining who communicates with whom at each round. A topological attention mixer incorporates the current directed topology into joint action-value factorization through utility weights conditioned on the global state and incoming and outgoing neighborhoods, enabling topology-aware temporal-difference (TD) credit assignment. Under a fixed pre-decision context, the monotonic mixer preserves Individual-Global-Max (IGM) consistency (Son et al., 2019), supporting decentralized greedy execution.

The main contributions are summarized as follows.

  • •

    Role-aware communication topology scheduling. ACTS combines communication-mode selection with role-aware relational attention to learn communication timing and variable-cardinality directed partner sets from agent roles and evolving local states. The scheduler jointly optimizes task performance and token efficiency.

  • •

    Topology-conditioned value factorization. A topological attention mixer learns nonnegative utility weights from the global state and directed incoming and outgoing neighborhoods for topology-aware TD credit assignment. The analysis relates graph-supported interactions to local joint-value sensitivities and establishes decentralized greedy consistency under a fixed pre-decision context.

  • •

    Accuracy and efficiency improvements. Evaluation covers nine benchmarks spanning four domains and two frozen backbone LLMs. Relative to Agent Q-Mix, ACTS improves macro-average accuracy by 3.183.18 and 6.196.19 percentage points and reduces average token consumption by 15.42%15.42\% and 13.84%13.84\% on GPT-OSS-120B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, respectively. Ablations and communication-pattern analyses further support the benefits of role embeddings, adaptive routing, and topological mixing.

2 Related Work

2.1 Communication and Topology Control

LLM-based multi-agent systems initially relied on fixed role-based workflows, structured debates, and predefined interaction templates, including CAMEL, AgentVerse, MetaGPT, ChatDev, AutoGen and LLM-Debate (Li et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2023; Qian et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2023; Du et al., 2023). Subsequent methods adapt interaction structures through graph induction, multi-agent architecture search, or agent-participation control, such as G-Designer, GPTSwarm, MaAS, Assemble Your Crew, AgentDropout, GTD, and TopoDIM (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026). These approaches generally do not jointly learn round-wise communication modes, directed partner selection, and topology-conditioned team-value evaluation. Agent Q-Mix introduces reinforcement-learning-based round-wise communication scheduling with a QMIX mixer (Jiang et al., 2026), but does not explicitly model agent roles or condition its value factorization on individual directed communication neighborhoods. ACTS addresses these limitations through role-aware relational attention and topological attention for directed partner selection and topology-aware value factorization.

2.2 Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

Cooperative MARL provides the optimization framework for decentralized decision-making under a shared team objective. Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) uses global information during training while restricting execution to local observations (Oliehoek & Amato, 2016). Value-factorization methods, including VDN, QMIX, QPLEX, and Qatten, represent the team value through individual utilities with different mixing structures (Sunehag et al., 2018; Rashid et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2020). Differentiable communication methods further study message passing and attention-based aggregation (Sukhbaatar et al., 2016; Foerster et al., 2016). ACTS builds on this foundation by learning discrete communication actions, role-aware interaction topologies, and topology-dependent utility weights within a CTDE framework.

3 ACTS: Dual-Attention Communication Topology Scheduling

ACTS is a CTDE framework for adaptive communication-topology scheduling in cooperative LLM agents (Oliehoek & Amato, 2016). It combines value-based mode selection with role-aware relational attention for directed partner selection, and incorporates the resulting topology into centralized value factorization through topological attention. Figure 2 illustrates the overall framework.

3.1 Problem Formulation

The proposed ACTS framework models adaptive communication topology scheduling as a cooperative multi-agent decision problem under CTDE (Rashid et al., 2018). Let ℐ={1,…,N}\mathcal{I}=\{1,\ldots,N\} denote the set of cooperative LLM agents, where agent ii is assigned a role ρi\rho_{i}. At round tt, agent ii receives a local observation oito_{i}^{t} and maintains a recurrent state hith_{i}^{t} encoding its interaction history. The global state sts^{t} is available only during centralized training.

Communication is represented by a directed graph Gt=(ℐ,ℰt)G^{t}=(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{E}^{t}), where (i,j)∈ℰt(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{t} denotes a communication link from agent ii to agent jj. We initialize G1G^{1} as the complete directed graph without self-loops and set ℐcomm1=ℐ\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{1}=\mathcal{I}. At round tt, the agents jointly select 𝒂t=(a1t,…,aNt)\bm{a}^{t}=(a_{1}^{t},\ldots,a_{N}^{t}) with ait∈𝒜comma_{i}^{t}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{comm}}. The communication-eligible set for the next round is

ℐcommt+1={i∈ℐ∣ait∉{aoff,asolo}}.\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t+1}=\left\{i\in\mathcal{I}\mid a_{i}^{t}\notin\{a^{\mathrm{off}},a^{\mathrm{solo}}\}\right\}. (1)

The selected modes and directional attention scores then determine the sender and receiver sets 𝒮it+1\mathcal{S}_{i}^{t+1} and ℛit+1\mathcal{R}_{i}^{t+1}, which define the directed topology Gt+1G^{t+1}.

For subsequent analysis, IG\operatorname{IG} (Cover & Thomas, 2006) denotes the topology-induced information gain, which measures the information-acquisition effectiveness of the topology scheduler. Let π\pi denote the topology-scheduling policy and ctokt​(τ)c_{\mathrm{tok}}^{t}(\tau) the token consumption at round tt along trajectory τ\tau. The policy is optimized to balance task performance and token efficiency:

π⋆=arg​maxπ⁡𝔼τ∼π​[wtask​Rtask​(τ)−wtok​min⁡(∑t=1Tctokt​(τ)B,1)],\pi^{\star}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\pi}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}\left[w_{\mathrm{task}}R_{\mathrm{task}}(\tau)-w_{\mathrm{tok}}\min\!\left(\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}c_{\mathrm{tok}}^{t}(\tau)}{B},1\right)\right], (2)

where Rtask​(τ)R_{\mathrm{task}}(\tau) denotes the final task score, BB is a token-cost normalization scale, and wtaskw_{\mathrm{task}} and wtokw_{\mathrm{tok}} control the trade-off between task performance and token efficiency.

3.2 Relational Attention for Communication Topology Learning

Existing topology schedulers rely on fixed communication patterns and do not explicitly model role-dependent partner relevance (Jiang et al., 2026). ACTS combines communication-mode selection with relational attention over recurrent representations that encode agent roles and evolving local contexts, thereby constructing adaptive directed neighborhoods with a variable number of partners.

At round tt, the GNN aggregates each agent’s local observation and role information according to the current topology GtG^{t}, while a GRU updates the recurrent state using the previous hidden state:

hit=GRUθh⁡(GNNθg⁡(oit,eρ​(ρi),Gt),hit−1),h_{i}^{t}=\operatorname{GRU}_{\theta_{h}}\!\left(\operatorname{GNN}_{\theta_{g}}\!\left(o_{i}^{t},e_{\rho}(\rho_{i}),G^{t}\right),h_{i}^{t-1}\right), (3)

where eρ​(ρi)e_{\rho}(\rho_{i}) denotes the embedding of agent ii’s role. The resulting states are processed by a cross-attention module, which computes the directed relevance between each ordered pair of agents:

αi​jt=softmaxj≠i⁡((WQ,rel​hit)⊤​(WK,rel​hjt)drel).\alpha_{ij}^{t}=\operatorname{softmax}_{j\neq i}\left(\frac{\left(W_{Q,\mathrm{rel}}h_{i}^{t}\right)^{\top}\left(W_{K,\mathrm{rel}}h_{j}^{t}\right)}{\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{rel}}}}\right). (4)

The ordered query–key construction produces directional attention weights, with αi​jt≠αj​it\alpha_{ij}^{t}\neq\alpha_{ji}^{t} in general. The cross-attention layer refines each recurrent state by aggregating value projections from other agents with a residual connection, producing the features used for local mode selection:

ξit=hit+∑j∈ℐ∖{i}αi​jt​WV,rel​hjt,ait=arg​maxa∈𝒜comm⁡Q​(ξit,a).\xi_{i}^{t}=h_{i}^{t}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}\setminus\{i\}}\alpha_{ij}^{t}W_{V,\mathrm{rel}}h_{j}^{t},\qquad a_{i}^{t}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{comm}}}Q(\xi_{i}^{t},a). (5)

The communication mode specifies the direction and scope of interaction, while relational attention selects the corresponding partners. For the eligible candidate set 𝒥it+1\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1}, the receiver and sender sets are

𝒮it+1\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{i}^{t+1} ={𝒥it+1,ait=abroadcast,{j∈𝒥it+1∣αi​jt>α¯iout,t},ait=aattn​-​broadcast,∅,otherwise,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1},&a_{i}^{t}=a^{\mathrm{broadcast}},\\ \{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1}\mid\alpha_{ij}^{t}>\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{\mathrm{out},t}\},&a_{i}^{t}=a^{\mathrm{attn\text{-}broadcast}},\\ \varnothing,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (6)
ℛit+1\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{i}^{t+1} ={𝒥it+1,ait=areceive,{j∈𝒥it+1∣αj​it>α¯iin,t},ait=aattn​-​receive,∅,otherwise.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1},&a_{i}^{t}=a^{\mathrm{receive}},\\ \{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1}\mid\alpha_{ji}^{t}>\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{\mathrm{in},t}\},&a_{i}^{t}=a^{\mathrm{attn\text{-}receive}},\\ \varnothing,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The resulting directed topology is

ℰt+1={(i,j)∈ℐ×ℐ|i≠j,j∈𝒮it+1∨i∈ℛjt+1},Gt+1=(ℐ,ℰt+1).\mathcal{E}^{t+1}=\left\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{I}\;\middle|\;i\neq j,\;j\in\mathcal{S}_{i}^{t+1}\ \lor\ i\in\mathcal{R}_{j}^{t+1}\right\},\qquad G^{t+1}=\left(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{E}^{t+1}\right). (7)

By incorporating role embeddings and topology-aware recurrent states, ACTS conditions both action evaluation and partner selection on the current agent context. This decoupled design enables directed, variable-cardinality topologies that adapt across rounds. The complete construction is given in Appendix B.

3.3 Topological Attention for Value Function Factorization

ACTS adopts CTDE value factorization with the Individual-Global-Max property for decentralized greedy execution (Sunehag et al., 2018; Rashid et al., 2018), as reviewed in Appendix A. The QMIX mixer in Agent Q-Mix does not explicitly encode individual directed communication neighborhoods. For a fixed pre-decision context, Appendix C.1 derives the local approximation

Qtott​(𝒂)≈bt+∑i∈ℐcommtβit​Qi​(ξit,ai),Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}(\bm{a})\approx b^{t}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\beta_{i}^{t}Q_{i}(\xi_{i}^{t},a_{i}), (8)

where βit\beta_{i}^{t} denotes the local sensitivity to agent ii’s utility under the global state sts^{t}. Under the graph interaction assumptions, the derivation relates this sensitivity to interactions within the incoming neighborhood 𝒩iin,t\mathcal{N}_{i}^{\mathrm{in},t} and outgoing neighborhood 𝒩iout,t\mathcal{N}_{i}^{\mathrm{out},t}. This motivates ACTS to learn nonnegative mixing coefficients through topological attention conditioned on the global state and separate representations of incoming and outgoing neighborhoods.

For each candidate communication action aia_{i}, ACTS encodes the directed neighborhoods in GtG^{t} by

zit\displaystyle z_{i}^{t} =Φθz(hit∥eρ(ρi)∥mi,int∥mi,outt),r∈{in,out}.\displaystyle=\Phi_{\theta_{z}}\left(h_{i}^{t}\mathbin{\|}e_{\rho}(\rho_{i})\mathbin{\|}m_{i,\mathrm{in}}^{t}\mathbin{\|}m_{i,\mathrm{out}}^{t}\right),\qquad r\in\{\mathrm{in},\mathrm{out}\}.

The topology representation zitz_{i}^{t}, used only by the centralized mixer, serves as the key in topological attention, while the global state sts^{t} provides the query. For each head hh, we first compute the attention logits and then normalize them over ℐcommt\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}:

ηi,ht\displaystyle\eta_{i,h}^{t} =(WQ,top(h)​st)⊤​(WK,top(h)​zit)dh,\displaystyle=\frac{\left(W_{Q,\mathrm{top}}^{(h)}s^{t}\right)^{\top}\left(W_{K,\mathrm{top}}^{(h)}z_{i}^{t}\right)}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}, λi,ht\displaystyle\lambda_{i,h}^{t} =[softmax⁡((ηj,ht)j∈ℐcommt)]i.\displaystyle=\left[\operatorname{softmax}\left(\left(\eta_{j,h}^{t}\right)_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\right)\right]_{i}. 3.4 Cooperative MARL Training and Execution

The training and execution procedures are detailed in Appendix D. During decentralized execution, agent ii selects ait=arg​maxa∈𝒜comm⁡Qi​(ξit,a)a_{i}^{t}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{comm}}}Q_{i}(\xi_{i}^{t},a), and the joint action 𝒂t=(a1t,…,aNt)\bm{a}^{t}=(a_{1}^{t},\ldots,a_{N}^{t}) induces the next-round topology Gt+1G^{t+1}. During centralized training, the mixer evaluates each replayed transition conditioned on its pre-decision state and topology, with the terminal team reward specified by  equation 2.

For each sampled transition, the target action of each communication-eligible agent is selected greedily:

ai∗,t+1=arg​maxa∈𝒜comm⁡Qi−​(ξit+1,a),i∈ℐcommt+1.a_{i}^{*,t+1}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{comm}}}Q_{i}^{-}(\xi_{i}^{t+1},a),\qquad i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t+1}. (13)

The TD target and loss are then defined as

yt\displaystyle y^{t} =rt+γ​Qtot−​(𝒂∗,t+1),\displaystyle=r^{t}+\gamma Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{-}\left(\bm{a}^{*,t+1}\right), (14)
ℒTD\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TD}} =𝔼𝒟​[(yt−Qtott​(𝒂t))2].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\left[\left(y^{t}-Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}(\bm{a}^{t})\right)^{2}\right].

The GNN, GRU, relational-attention module, local action-value networks, topology encoder, and topological mixer are optimized jointly, while the backbone LLM remains frozen. For terminal transitions, the target is yt=rty^{t}=r^{t}. Mixer coefficients are computed from the fixed pre-decision context, and the discrete topology transition is excluded from gradient computation.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate ACTS on nine benchmarks spanning four domains: code generation (LiveCodeBench v6 and HumanEval), multiple-choice reasoning (MMLU-Pro and the first 250 questions of Humanity’s Last Exam), multi-hop question answering (HotpotQA), and competition mathematics (AIME 2025/2026, HMMT 2025, and Beyond-AIME) (Jain et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024; Phan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2018; Mathematical Association of America, 2025; Mathematical Association of America, 2026; MathArena, 2025; ByteDance-Seed, 2025). We use GPT-OSS-120B (OpenAI, 2025) and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) as frozen backbone LLMs; each task instantiates three role-conditioned agents and a final answer-aggregation node. Baselines include direct prompting, fixed or framework-based coordination (LLM-Debate, AutoGen, LangGraph, and Agent Framework), task-adaptive topology scheduling (TopoDIM), and MARL-based topology scheduling (Agent Q-Mix) (Du et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; LangChain AI, 2024; Sun et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2026). All methods use the same prompts, team size, communication-round budget, and evaluation protocol. Results are averaged over three independent random seeds. Detailed benchmark, baseline, and training configurations are provided in Appendix E.1.

4.2 Main Results

Accuracy gains from selective communication. Table 1 reports accuracy across all nine benchmarks. ACTS achieves the highest average accuracy on both backbone models, 75.01%75.01\% on GPT-OSS-120B and 69.43%69.43\% on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, exceeding Agent Q-Mix by 3.183.18 and 6.196.19 points in each case, and attains the best or tied-best result on every benchmark. This advantage is concentrated on tasks where agents hold complementary information, because relational attention selects communication partners by semantic relevance rather than by fixed topology or content-agnostic index rules.

Pareto-optimal efficiency across IG regimes. Figure 4 plots accuracy against token consumption on HotpotQA (IG>0\mathrm{IG}>0) and HLE (IG≈0\mathrm{IG}\approx 0); full counts are provided in Table 4 (Appendix E.5). Static topologies broadcast every round regardless of whether communication is useful; centralized adaptive topologies adjust the structure only at generation time, not during execution. Agent Q-Mix learns agent deactivation and primitive-based routing, but discrete communication primitives provide limited selectivity. ACTS achieves Pareto optimality across all four settings: it matches or exceeds Agent Q-Mix at lower token cost and dominates static and centralized families on both accuracy and cost. Only single-agent prompting uses fewer tokens, at an accuracy cost of approximately 2727 percentage points on HotpotQA with GPT-OSS-120B. On HLE, where information gain is near zero, ACTS and single-agent prompting yield comparable performance. By learning whether communication is warranted and routing through attention affinities, ACTS spends tokens only where expected information gain justifies the expenditure.

4.3 Experimental Analysis

4.3.1 Information Gain Analysis

Information gain (IG) (Cover & Thomas, 2006) governs whether communication confers an advantage: agents benefit only when they contribute complementary evidence. Figure 5 compares mean accuracy gains across topology families relative to single-agent prompting. Uplift falls below the sampling-noise threshold x=2/nx=2/n on HLE and with limited-capacity DeepSeek-V4-Flash on HMMT, yielding null IG. It surpasses this threshold on HotpotQAand contest math, where cross-entity evidence and divergent solution paths engender separable signals, yielding positive IG. ACTS navigates both regimes: attention-driven partner selection amplifies communication when IG is positive; single-agent inference when null.

4.3.2 Communication Pattern Analysis

ACTS achieves its gains through attention-gated selective communication and dynamic deactivation, two complementary mechanisms analyzed on HotpotQA and HLE, two settings that respectively exhibit high and negligible IG\mathrm{IG}. At each round the agent network computes asymmetric directional scores αi​jt\alpha_{ij}^{t}; attn-broadcast retains edge i→ji\!\to\!j when αi​jt\alpha_{ij}^{t} exceeds the mean over eligible candidates, attn-receive retains j→ij\!\to\!i under the symmetric condition on αj​it\alpha_{ji}^{t}, and together these actions construct sparse neighborhoods specific to each round in place of a fixed topology. Trained end to end with the joint accuracy and token objective, the attention module suppresses redundant interactions, as quantified in Table 4 of Appendix E.5. Independently, the off action deactivates an agent by suppressing its LLM call and outgoing edges; when a majority of agents become inactive the episode terminates early, forgoing rounds unlikely to alter the answer, whereas agents persist when broader collaboration is warranted, and consequently tasks requiring limited collaboration incur cost approaching that of a single agent. Figure 6 contrasts the learned action distributions under DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Under high IG, off stays at 4.2%4.2\% whereas broadcast reaches 22.7%22.7\%; under IG near zero, off rises to 21.3%21.3\%, broadcast and attn-broadcast drop to 12.1%12.1\% and 6.4%6.4\%, and attn-receive dominates at 28.3%28.3\%. Appendix E.4 provides a comparison of the two regimes at the trajectory level.

4.3.3 Ablation Studies

Table 2 isolates the three components distinguishing ACTS from Agent Q-Mix (Jiang et al., 2026). Replacing the topological attention mixer with QMIX (Rashid et al., 2018) induces the strongest degradation, lowering macro-average accuracy from 75.01%75.01\% to 71.83%71.83\% on GPT-OSS-120B (OpenAI, 2025) and from 69.43%69.43\% to 63.24%63.24\% on DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), with token usage rising from 5.975.97 to 7.417.41 and from 4.034.03 to 4.964.96. These results support the effectiveness of the proposed topological attention mixer relative to the QMIX replacement under the evaluated settings. Substituting fixed role-based partners for learned relational routing reduces accuracy to 72.50%72.50\% and 66.10%66.10\% and raises token usage to 8.108.10 and 6.206.20, the largest overhead among the variants, as fixed assignments cannot adapt partner selection to the task. With role-specific LLM prompts retained, removing role embeddings from relational attention reduces macro-average accuracy to 73.40%73.40\% and 67.10%67.10\% and increases token usage to 6.80×1036.80\times 10^{3} and 4.60×1034.60\times 10^{3} on GPT-OSS-120B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, respectively. These results support the contribution of explicit role conditioning to task performance and communication efficiency.

5 Conclusion

We introduced ACTS, a role-aware adaptive communication-topology scheduling framework for efficient LLM-based multi-agent collaboration. Under CTDE, its dual-attention design jointly learns when communication should occur and which directed agent pairs should exchange information: role-aware relational attention selects variable-cardinality partners from agent roles and evolving execution states, while a topological attention mixer incorporates the realized directed topology into team-value factorization for topology-aware credit assignment. Across nine benchmarks and two frozen backbone LLMs, ACTS improves the accuracy–efficiency trade-off over Agent Q-Mix by up to 6.196.19 percentage points in accuracy and up to 15.42%15.42\% in token reduction. These results demonstrate the benefit of learning communication modes and directed partner relations jointly for efficient role-aware LLM collaboration.

Appendix A Value Function Factorization in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

A.1 Centralized Training with Decentralized Execution

Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) considers a set of agents that jointly maximize a shared return. Let sts^{t} denote the global state, τit\tau_{i}^{t} the local action-observation history of agent ii, and 𝒖t=(u1t,…,uNt)\bm{u}^{t}=(u_{1}^{t},\ldots,u_{N}^{t}) the joint action. The objective is

J⁡(π)=𝔼π​[∑t=1Tγt−1​rt],J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{t-1}r^{t}\right], (15)

where rtr^{t} is the shared reward and γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1) is the discount factor.

In partially observable environments, each agent makes decisions from its local action-observation history. Independent value-based learning is challenging because the joint action space grows exponentially with the number of agents, while the effective environment of each agent changes as the other agents update their policies. Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) addresses these issues by allowing the training procedure to access centralized information, while restricting execution to local histories.

Let Qi​(τit,ui)Q_{i}(\tau_{i}^{t},u_{i}) denote the individual action-value function of agent ii. Under CTDE, the centralized joint action-value function can be represented as

Qtot​(st,𝝉t,𝒖t)=Fψ​(st,{Qi​(τit,uit)}i=1N),Q_{\mathrm{tot}}\left(s^{t},\bm{\tau}^{t},\bm{u}^{t}\right)=F_{\psi}\left(s^{t},\left\{Q_{i}(\tau_{i}^{t},u_{i}^{t})\right\}_{i=1}^{N}\right), (16)

where FψF_{\psi} is a centralized factorization function. This formulation allows centralized training to model inter-agent dependencies while retaining decentralized action selection at execution time.

A.2 Value Function Factorization

Value Decomposition Networks (VDN) use the additive factorization

Qtot​(𝝉,𝒖)=∑i=1NQi​(τi,ui),Q_{\mathrm{tot}}\left(\bm{\tau},\bm{u}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}Q_{i}(\tau_{i},u_{i}), (17)

which supports decentralized execution but cannot represent general non-additive interactions among agents (Sunehag et al., 2018).

QMIX introduces a nonlinear factorization function (Rashid et al., 2018):

Qtot=Fψ​(Q1,…,QN,s),Q_{\mathrm{tot}}=F_{\psi}\left(Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{N};s\right), (18)

subject to the monotonicity condition

∂Qtot∂Qi≥0,i=1,…,N.\frac{\partial Q_{\mathrm{tot}}}{\partial Q_{i}}\geq 0,\qquad i=1,\ldots,N. (19)

Thus, increasing an individual utility cannot decrease the joint value when the remaining utilities and the centralized state are fixed. QMIX typically enforces this condition by generating nonnegative factorization weights from the global state through hypernetworks.

Subsequent methods improve the expressiveness of value function factorization in different ways. QTRAN introduces transformation and consistency constraints to represent a broader class of joint value functions (Son et al., 2019). QPLEX uses a duplex dueling architecture to construct a more expressive value–advantage factorization while preserving decentralized consistency (Wang et al., 2021). Attention- based factorization methods assign context-dependent weights to individual utilities, allowing their contributions to vary with the centralized context (Yang et al., 2020).

A.3 Monotonic Value Mixing and the IGM Property

A factorized joint action-value function satisfies the Individual–Global–Max (IGM) (Sunehag et al., 2018; Rashid et al., 2018; Son et al., 2019) property if its globally greedy action is consistent with the individual greedy actions:

arg​max𝒖⁡Qtot​(s,𝝉,𝒖)=(arg​maxu1⁡Q1​(τ1,u1),…,arg​maxuN⁡QN​(τN,uN)).\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\bm{u}}Q_{\mathrm{tot}}\left(s,\bm{\tau},\bm{u}\right)=\left(\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{u_{1}}Q_{1}(\tau_{1},u_{1}),\ldots,\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{u_{N}}Q_{N}(\tau_{N},u_{N})\right). (20)

With consistent tie-breaking, this property means that the globally optimal joint action can be recovered by independently maximizing the individual action-value functions.

Componentwise monotonicity is a sufficient condition for IGM. For fixed ss and 𝝉\bm{\tau}, consider two joint actions that differ only in agent ii’s action. If one action produces a larger value of Qi​(τi,ui)Q_{i}(\tau_{i},u_{i}), the monotonicity condition ensures that it cannot produce a smaller value of QtotQ_{\mathrm{tot}}. Applying this argument coordinate-wise to all agents shows that independent greedy action selection yields a globally optimal joint action.

A.4 Temporal-Difference Optimization

Cooperative value function factorization methods are commonly trained with a centralized temporal-difference objective while retaining decentralized execution (Sunehag et al., 2018; Rashid et al., 2018; Son et al., 2019). For a transition (st,𝝉t,𝒖t,rt,st+1,dt)(s^{t},\bm{\tau}^{t},\bm{u}^{t},r^{t},s^{t+1},d^{t}), where dtd^{t} indicates episode termination, a target network forms

yt=rt+γ⁡(1−dt)​Qtot−​(st+1,𝝉t+1,𝒖∗,t+1).y^{t}=r^{t}+\gamma(1-d^{t})Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{-}\left(s^{t+1},\bm{\tau}^{t+1},\bm{u}^{*,t+1}\right). (21)

When the factorization satisfies the Individual–Global-Max property, the target joint action can be selected independently (Rashid et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021):

ui∗,t+1=arg​maxuiQi−(τit+1,ui),i=1,…,N.u_{i}^{*,t+1}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{u_{i}}Q_{i}^{-}\left(\tau_{i}^{t+1},u_{i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N. (22)

The online parameters are optimized by minimizing

ℒTD=𝔼𝒟​[(yt−Qtot​(st,𝝉t,𝒖t))2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TD}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\left[\left(y^{t}-Q_{\mathrm{tot}}\left(s^{t},\bm{\tau}^{t},\bm{u}^{t}\right)\right)^{2}\right]. (23)

Experience replay and delayed target networks are commonly used to stabilize optimization under deep function approximation (Rashid et al., 2018; Son et al., 2019).

Appendix B Construction of the Directed Communication Topology

This section gives the complete construction of Gt+1=Ψ⁡(𝒂t,𝜶t)G^{t+1}=\Psi(\bm{a}^{t},\bm{\alpha}^{t}). After communication-mode selection, define the communication-eligible agents and candidate partners as

ℐt+1comm={i∈ℐ|ait∉{aoff,asolo}},𝒥it+1=ℐt+1comm∖{i}.\mathcal{I}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{comm}}=\left\{i\in\mathcal{I}\;\middle|\;a_{i}^{t}\notin\left\{a^{\mathrm{off}},a^{\mathrm{solo}}\right\}\right\},\qquad\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1}=\mathcal{I}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{comm}}\setminus\{i\}. (24)

The index t+1t+1 indicates that these sets determine the topology produced by the decisions at round tt.

For i∈ℐt+1commi\in\mathcal{I}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{comm}} with 𝒥it+1≠∅\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1}\neq\varnothing, define the outgoing and incoming mean scores as

α¯iout,t=1|𝒥it+1|​∑j∈𝒥it+1αi​jt,α¯iin,t=1|𝒥it+1|​∑j∈𝒥it+1αj​it.\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{\mathrm{out},t}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1}}\alpha_{ij}^{t},\qquad\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{\mathrm{in},t}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1}}\alpha_{ji}^{t}. (25)

The requested receiver and sender sets are

𝒮it+1\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{i}^{t+1} ={𝒥it+1,ait=abroadcast,{j∈𝒥it+1|αi​jt>α¯iout,t},ait=aattn​-​broadcast,∅,otherwise,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1},&a_{i}^{t}=a^{\mathrm{broadcast}},\\ \left\{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1}\;\middle|\;\alpha_{ij}^{t}>\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{\mathrm{out},t}\right\},&a_{i}^{t}=a^{\mathrm{attn\text{-}broadcast}},\\ \varnothing,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (26)
ℛit+1\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{i}^{t+1} ={𝒥it+1,ait=areceive,{j∈𝒥it+1|αj​it>α¯iin,t},ait=aattn​-​receive,∅,otherwise.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1},&a_{i}^{t}=a^{\mathrm{receive}},\\ \left\{j\in\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1}\;\middle|\;\alpha_{ji}^{t}>\bar{\alpha}_{i}^{\mathrm{in},t}\right\},&a_{i}^{t}=a^{\mathrm{attn\text{-}receive}},\\ \varnothing,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

When 𝒥it+1=∅\mathcal{J}_{i}^{t+1}=\varnothing, both request sets are defined as empty.

The directed edge set is then

ℰt+1={(i,j)∈ℐt+1comm×ℐt+1comm|i≠j,j∈𝒮it+1∨i∈ℛjt+1},\mathcal{E}^{t+1}=\left\{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{comm}}\times\mathcal{I}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{comm}}\;\middle|\;i\neq j,\;j\in\mathcal{S}_{i}^{t+1}\lor i\in\mathcal{R}_{j}^{t+1}\right\}, (27)

and

Gt+1=(ℐ,ℰt+1).G^{t+1}=\left(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{E}^{t+1}\right). (28)

Thus, abroadcasta^{\mathrm{broadcast}} and areceivea^{\mathrm{receive}} request all eligible interactions in the corresponding direction, whereas aattn​-​broadcasta^{\mathrm{attn\text{-}broadcast}} and aattn​-​receivea^{\mathrm{attn\text{-}receive}} retain only interactions whose scores exceed the corresponding mean. The strict mean threshold allows the number of selected partners to adapt to the score distribution without introducing a fixed top-kk hyperparameter.

Appendix C Theoretical Analysis of Topological Value Factorization

At a non-terminal round tt, let ℐcommt≠∅\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}\neq\varnothing denote the set of agents eligible to make communication decisions, fixed before the current actions are selected. The corresponding pre-decision context is

𝒞t=(st,Gt,ℐcommt,{ξit,zit}i∈ℐcommt),\mathcal{C}^{t}=\left(s^{t},\;G^{t},\;\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t},\;\{\xi_{i}^{t},z_{i}^{t}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\right), (29)

where ξit\xi_{i}^{t} is the input to the individual action-value function and zitz_{i}^{t} encodes agent ii’s directed neighborhoods in GtG^{t} for centralized value factorization. Let 𝒂t=(ait)i∈ℐ\bm{a}^{t}=(a_{i}^{t})_{i\in\mathcal{I}} denote the full joint action, with ait=aoffa_{i}^{t}=a^{\mathrm{off}} for every i∉ℐcommti\notin\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}. The selected actions determine

ℐcommt+1={i∈ℐ:ait∉{aoff,asolo}},Gt+1=Ψ⁡(𝒞t,𝒂t),\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t+1}=\left\{i\in\mathcal{I}:\;a_{i}^{t}\notin\{a^{\mathrm{off}},a^{\mathrm{solo}}\}\right\},\qquad G^{t+1}=\Psi\!\left(\mathcal{C}^{t},\bm{a}^{t}\right), (30)

where Ψ\Psi denotes the construction of Appendix B. Because every agent outside ℐcommt\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t} is assigned aoffa^{\mathrm{off}}, Equation 30 implies ℐcommt+1⊆ℐcommt\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t+1}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}: the eligible set contracts monotonically along an episode, so an agent that selects aoffa^{\mathrm{off}} or asoloa^{\mathrm{solo}} withdraws from communication for the remainder of the episode.

C.1 Local Expansion and Interaction-Dependent Coefficients

Fix 𝒞t\mathcal{C}^{t} and let 𝒒=(qi)i∈ℐcommt\bm{q}=(q_{i})_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}} denote a vector of individual utility values. Suppose a reference joint action-value function is represented locally by a map

F𝒞t​(𝒒)=cref,t+∑i∈ℐcommtβiref,t​qi+R2t.F_{\mathcal{C}^{t}}(\bm{q})=c^{\mathrm{ref},t}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\beta_{i}^{\mathrm{ref},t}q_{i}+R_{2}^{t}. (33)

|R2t|≤L2​‖𝒒−𝒒¯‖22.\left|R_{2}^{t}\right|\leq\frac{L}{2}\left\|\bm{q}-\bar{\bm{q}}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (34)

Remark C.2.

Proposition C.1 is a statement about the form of a local approximation rather than a claim of novelty: every C2C^{2} reference value admits weighted-sum coefficients equal to its local sensitivities. Its role here is to identify what a mixer must supply, namely per-agent coefficients that vary with the pre-decision context, and to bound the error of the weighted-sum form by the curvature of F𝒞tF_{\mathcal{C}^{t}}. The analysis that follows concerns which quantities those coefficients depend on.

The coefficient βiref,t\beta_{i}^{\mathrm{ref},t} is the local sensitivity of the reference joint value to agent ii’s utility, and its variation across operating points is governed by mixed derivatives. Applying the fundamental theorem of calculus to u↦∂iF𝒞t​(𝒒¯+u​𝜹)u\mapsto\partial_{i}F_{\mathcal{C}^{t}}(\bar{\bm{q}}+u\bm{\delta}) and using the chain rule gives, for any displacement 𝜹\bm{\delta} whose segment lies in 𝒰\mathcal{U},

βiref,t​(𝒒¯+𝜹)−βiref,t​(𝒒¯)=∑j∈ℐcommtδj​∫01∂i​jF𝒞t​(𝒒¯+u​𝜹)​𝑑u.\beta_{i}^{\mathrm{ref},t}(\bar{\bm{q}}+\bm{\delta})-\beta_{i}^{\mathrm{ref},t}(\bar{\bm{q}})=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\delta_{j}\int_{0}^{1}\partial_{ij}F_{\mathcal{C}^{t}}(\bar{\bm{q}}+u\bm{\delta})\,du. (36)

For j≠ij\neq i, the mixed derivative ∂i​jF𝒞t\partial_{ij}F_{\mathcal{C}^{t}} characterizes how agent jj’s utility affects the joint value’s local sensitivity to agent ii’s utility. This dependence motivates context-dependent mixing coefficients, consistent with attention-based value factorization (Yang et al., 2020).

A direct connection to the communication neighborhoods follows once the reference value is graph structured. Let

ℰcommt=ℰt∩(ℐcommt×ℐcommt),𝒩iout,t={j:(i,j)∈ℰcommt},𝒩iin,t={j:(j,i)∈ℰcommt}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}=\mathcal{E}^{t}\cap\left(\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}\times\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}\right),\quad\mathcal{N}_{i}^{\mathrm{out},t}=\{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}\},\quad\mathcal{N}_{i}^{\mathrm{in},t}=\{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}\} (37)

denote the directed, self-loop-free edge set induced on ℐcommt\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t} and the associated neighborhoods. Agents that exchange no messages at round tt influence one another only through the shared team reward, so modelling the interaction terms of the reference value as supported on ℰcommt\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t} is the natural structural assumption.

Proposition C.3 (Graph-supported coefficients).

Let 𝒮⁡(Gt)\mathcal{S}(G^{t}) be a collection of scopes S⊆ℐcommtS\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t} supported on GtG^{t}, write 𝐪S=(qj)j∈S\bm{q}_{S}=(q_{j})_{j\in S}, and suppose

F𝒞t​(𝒒)=a𝒞t+∑S∈𝒮⁡(Gt)fS​(𝒒S,Gt),F_{\mathcal{C}^{t}}(\bm{q})=a_{\mathcal{C}^{t}}+\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}(G^{t})}f_{S}(\bm{q}_{S};G^{t}), (38)

with every fSf_{S} continuously differentiable in its arguments. Then

βiref,t​(𝒒)=∑S∈𝒮⁡(Gt)i∈S∂ifS​(𝒒S,Gt).\beta_{i}^{\mathrm{ref},t}(\bm{q})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\in\mathcal{S}(G^{t})\\ i\in S\end{subarray}}\partial_{i}f_{S}(\bm{q}_{S};G^{t}). (39)
Proof.

Differentiating Equation 38 with respect to qiq_{i} annihilates a𝒞ta_{\mathcal{C}^{t}} and every factor whose scope does not contain ii, since such factors do not depend on qiq_{i}. Summing the derivatives of the remaining factors gives Equation 39. ∎

Proposition C.3 places no restriction on the cardinality of the scopes, so every graph-induced interaction factor containing agent ii, including higher-order ones, can contribute to its coefficient. The pairwise case isolates the two directed contributions.

Corollary C.4 (Directed-neighborhood dependence).

Suppose

F𝒞t​(𝒒)=a𝒞t+∑i∈ℐcommtfi​(qi)+∑(i,j)∈ℰcommtfi​j​(qi,qj).F_{\mathcal{C}^{t}}(\bm{q})=a_{\mathcal{C}^{t}}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}f_{i}(q_{i})+\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}f_{ij}(q_{i},q_{j}). (40)

Then

βiref,t​(𝒒)=\displaystyle\beta_{i}^{\mathrm{ref},t}(\bm{q})={} fi′​(qi)+∑j∈𝒩iout,t∂1fi​j​(qi,qj)\displaystyle f_{i}^{\prime}(q_{i})+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{\mathrm{out},t}}\partial_{1}f_{ij}(q_{i},q_{j}) (41)
+∑j∈𝒩iin,t∂2fj​i(qj,qi).\displaystyle+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{i}^{\mathrm{in},t}}\partial_{2}f_{ji}(q_{j},q_{i}).
Proof.

Apply Proposition C.3 with 𝒮⁡(Gt)={{i}:i∈ℐcommt}∪ℰcommt\mathcal{S}(G^{t})=\{\{i\}:i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}\}\cup\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}. The unary scope containing ii contributes fi′​(qi)f_{i}^{\prime}(q_{i}). Because ℰcommt\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t} is directed and self-loop free, a pairwise scope contains ii in exactly one of two ways: for an outgoing edge (i,j)(i,j) the utility qiq_{i} occupies the first argument of fi​jf_{ij}, and for an incoming edge (j,i)(j,i) it occupies the second argument of fj​if_{ji}. Summing the corresponding partial derivatives gives Equation 41. ∎

Corollary C.4 is the design justification for the topology encoder of Equation 9. The incoming and outgoing neighborhoods enter βiref,t\beta_{i}^{\mathrm{ref},t} through distinct partial derivatives, ∂2fj​i\partial_{2}f_{ji} and ∂1fi​j\partial_{1}f_{ij} respectively, so a representation that merges them into a single undirected neighborhood conflates two terms that are not interchangeable. A representation built from graph-level statistics such as edge count or density is weaker still: it discards the identity of agent ii and therefore cannot express the restriction to scopes containing ii that Equation 39 imposes. ACTS accordingly encodes both directed neighborhoods in zitz_{i}^{t}. It does not evaluate βiref,t\beta_{i}^{\mathrm{ref},t} analytically; it learns a nonnegative surrogate β^it\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t} from TD targets, as described next.

C.2 Topology-Aware TD Credit Assignment

For i∈ℐcommti\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t} define the individual utility and the topological-attention logit of head hh,

Qit​(ai)=Qi​(ξit,ai),ηi,ht=(WQ,top(h)​st)⊤​(WK,top(h)​zit)dh,Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i})=Q_{i}(\xi_{i}^{t},a_{i}),\qquad\eta_{i,h}^{t}=\frac{\left(W_{Q,\mathrm{top}}^{(h)}s^{t}\right)^{\top}\left(W_{K,\mathrm{top}}^{(h)}z_{i}^{t}\right)}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}, (42)

with weights normalized over the eligible agents,

λi,ht=exp⁡(ηi,ht)∑j∈ℐcommtexp⁡(ηj,ht).\lambda_{i,h}^{t}=\frac{\exp\!\left(\eta_{i,h}^{t}\right)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\exp\!\left(\eta_{j,h}^{t}\right)}. (43)

Let wht=|[fθw​(st)]h|≥0w_{h}^{t}=\left|\left[f_{\theta_{w}}(s^{t})\right]_{h}\right|\geq 0 be the nonnegative head weights and bt=Vθb​(st)b^{t}=V_{\theta_{b}}(s^{t}) the state-dependent bias. The head-level and joint action values are

Qht​(𝒂)\displaystyle Q_{h}^{t}(\bm{a}) =∑i∈ℐcommtλi,ht​Qit​(ai),\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\lambda_{i,h}^{t}Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i}), (44)
Qtott​(𝒞t,𝒂)\displaystyle Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}(\mathcal{C}^{t},\bm{a}) =bt+∑h=1Hwht​Qht​(𝒂)=bt+∑i∈ℐcommtβ^it​Qit​(ai),\displaystyle=b^{t}+\sum_{h=1}^{H}w_{h}^{t}Q_{h}^{t}(\bm{a})=b^{t}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i}),

where the effective mixing coefficient is

β^it=∑h=1Hwht​λi,ht≥ 0.\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}=\sum_{h=1}^{H}w_{h}^{t}\lambda_{i,h}^{t}\;\geq\;0. (45)

The second equality in Equation 44 follows by exchanging the two finite sums, and shows that the multi-head mixer is, for a fixed context, a nonnegatively weighted sum of individual utilities whose weights are determined by {zit}\{z_{i}^{t}\} and hence by GtG^{t}.

Remark C.5 (Functional form of a head).

Since sts^{t} is shared by all agents within a head, Equation 42 can be written as ηi,ht=⟨vh​(st),zit⟩\eta_{i,h}^{t}=\langle v_{h}(s^{t}),z_{i}^{t}\rangle with vh​(st)=(WK,top(h))⊤​WQ,top(h)​st/dhv_{h}(s^{t})=(W_{K,\mathrm{top}}^{(h)})^{\top}W_{Q,\mathrm{top}}^{(h)}s^{t}/\sqrt{d_{h}}. Each head therefore contributes one state-dependent linear direction in neighborhood-embedding space along which agents are compared, and whtw_{h}^{t} determines how much that direction matters in the current state.

For a sampled transition let yty^{t} denote the detached TD target and set

δt=Qtott​(𝒞t,𝒂t)−yt,ℓTDt=12​(δt)2.\delta^{t}=Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}(\mathcal{C}^{t},\bm{a}^{t})-y^{t},\qquad\ell_{\mathrm{TD}}^{t}=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\delta^{t}\right)^{2}. (46)
Proposition C.6 (Topology-aware TD gradients).

Conditional on the context 𝒞t\mathcal{C}^{t} and with yty^{t} treated as a constant,

∂ℓTDt∂Qit​(ait)=δt​β^it,∂ℓTDt∂wht=δt​Qht​(𝒂t),\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{TD}}^{t}}{\partial Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i}^{t})}=\delta^{t}\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t},\qquad\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{TD}}^{t}}{\partial w_{h}^{t}}=\delta^{t}Q_{h}^{t}(\bm{a}^{t}), (47)

and for every eligible agent ii and head hh,

∂ℓTDt∂ηi,ht=δt​wht​λi,ht​(Qit​(ait)−Qht​(𝒂t)).\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{TD}}^{t}}{\partial\eta_{i,h}^{t}}=\delta^{t}w_{h}^{t}\lambda_{i,h}^{t}\left(Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i}^{t})-Q_{h}^{t}(\bm{a}^{t})\right). (48)
Proof.

equation 44 gives ∂Qtott/∂Qit​(ait)=β^it\partial Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}/\partial Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i}^{t})=\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t} and ∂Qtott/∂wht=Qht​(𝒂t)\partial Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}/\partial w_{h}^{t}=Q_{h}^{t}(\bm{a}^{t}); since ∂ℓTDt/∂Qtott=δt\partial\ell_{\mathrm{TD}}^{t}/\partial Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}=\delta^{t} when yty^{t} is detached, the chain rule yields Equation 47. For the logits, the softmax Jacobian of Equation 43 is

∂λj,ht∂ηi,ht=λj,ht(𝕀[i=j]−λi,ht),\frac{\partial\lambda_{j,h}^{t}}{\partial\eta_{i,h}^{t}}=\lambda_{j,h}^{t}\left(\mathbb{I}[i=j]-\lambda_{i,h}^{t}\right),

and ηi,ht\eta_{i,h}^{t} enters only head hh, so

∂Qht​(𝒂t)∂ηi,ht=∑j∈ℐcommtQjt(ajt)λj,ht(𝕀[i=j]−λi,ht)=λi,ht(Qit(ait)−Qht(𝒂t)),\frac{\partial Q_{h}^{t}(\bm{a}^{t})}{\partial\eta_{i,h}^{t}}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}Q_{j}^{t}(a_{j}^{t})\lambda_{j,h}^{t}\left(\mathbb{I}[i=j]-\lambda_{i,h}^{t}\right)=\lambda_{i,h}^{t}\left(Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i}^{t})-Q_{h}^{t}(\bm{a}^{t})\right),

where the last step uses ∑jλj,ht​Qjt​(ajt)=Qht​(𝒂t)\sum_{j}\lambda_{j,h}^{t}Q_{j}^{t}(a_{j}^{t})=Q_{h}^{t}(\bm{a}^{t}). Combining with ∂Qtott/∂Qht=wht\partial Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}/\partial Q_{h}^{t}=w_{h}^{t} proves Equation 48. ∎

equation 47 shows that β^it\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t} is simultaneously the Jacobian of the mixer with respect to agent ii’s selected utility and the scale of the direct TD signal that this utility receives: monotonicity and credit assignment are governed by the same quantity. Because β^it\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t} depends on zitz_{i}^{t}, and zitz_{i}^{t} encodes the directed neighborhoods of GtG^{t} by Corollary C.4, the allocation is topology aware.  equation 48 has the form of an advantage: the deviation Qit−QhtQ_{i}^{t}-Q_{h}^{t} compares agent ii’s utility against the weighted mean of head hh, so a head increases its weight on agents whose utility exceeds that mean whenever the joint value must increase (δt<0\delta^{t}<0), and decreases it otherwise. The head weights are produced by an absolute value and are therefore differentiable except on the measure-zero set [fθw​(st)]h=0[f_{\theta_{w}}(s^{t})]_{h}=0, where the subgradient is taken to be zero, as is standard for monotonic mixers (Rashid et al., 2018).

Remark C.7 (Where credit for partner selection enters).

All quantities in Equation 44 are computed from the pre-decision context, so QtottQ_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t} does not depend on the topology Gt+1G^{t+1} that 𝐚t\bm{a}^{t} induces, and the discrete map Ψ\Psi of Equation 30 is never differentiated. Credit for a partner configuration is consequently not delivered within round tt; it is delivered through the TD target, because Qtott+1Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t+1} is conditioned on 𝒞t+1\mathcal{C}^{t+1} and hence on Gt+1G^{t+1}. A partner set that improves the team’s subsequent value raises yty^{t} and, through Equation 47, increases Qit​(ait)Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i}^{t}) for the actions that produced it. Relational attention additionally receives gradient within round tt along a differentiable path, since the aggregated feature ξit\xi_{i}^{t} of Equation 5 enters QitQ_{i}^{t} directly.

C.3 Monotonicity and Individual–Global–Max Consistency

Let each eligible agent have a finite, nonempty action space 𝒜it⊆𝒜comm\mathcal{A}_{i}^{t}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{comm}} and write

𝒜t=∏i∈ℐcommt𝒜it.\mathcal{A}^{t}=\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\mathcal{A}_{i}^{t}. (49)

The context and the mixing coefficients are held fixed while the elements of 𝒜t\mathcal{A}^{t} are compared. In particular aoffa^{\mathrm{off}} and asoloa^{\mathrm{solo}} are ordinary candidates: their effect is realized in ℐcommt+1\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t+1} and Gt+1G^{t+1} through Equation 30, not in the current attention normalization. By Equation 45,

∂Qtott∂Qit​(ai)=β^it≥ 0∀i∈ℐcommt,\frac{\partial Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}}{\partial Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i})}=\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}\;\geq\;0\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}, (50)

so the mixer is monotonic in every individual utility. Define

ℳit=arg​maxai∈𝒜it⁡Qit​(ai),𝒫t={i:β^it>0},𝒵t={i:β^it=0}.\mathcal{M}_{i}^{t}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{i}^{t}}Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i}),\qquad\mathcal{P}^{t}=\left\{i:\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}>0\right\},\qquad\mathcal{Z}^{t}=\left\{i:\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}=0\right\}. (51)
Theorem C.8 (IGM consistency).

For the fixed context 𝒞t\mathcal{C}^{t},

arg​max𝒂∈𝒜t⁡Qtott​(𝒞t,𝒂)=(∏i∈𝒫tℳit)×(∏i∈𝒵t𝒜it),\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\bm{a}\in\mathcal{A}^{t}}Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}(\mathcal{C}^{t},\bm{a})=\left(\prod_{i\in\mathcal{P}^{t}}\mathcal{M}_{i}^{t}\right)\times\left(\prod_{i\in\mathcal{Z}^{t}}\mathcal{A}_{i}^{t}\right), (52)

so every independently greedy joint action is a joint maximizer. If in addition the attention logits are finite and

Wt:=∑h=1Hwht> 0,W^{t}:=\sum_{h=1}^{H}w_{h}^{t}\;>\;0, (53)

then β^it>0\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}>0 for every i∈ℐcommti\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t} and the set-valued IGM identity holds exactly:

arg​max𝒂∈𝒜t⁡Qtott​(𝒞t,𝒂)=∏i∈ℐcommtarg​maxai∈𝒜it⁡Qi​(ξit,ai).\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\bm{a}\in\mathcal{A}^{t}}Q_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}(\mathcal{C}^{t},\bm{a})=\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{i}^{t}}Q_{i}(\xi_{i}^{t},a_{i}). (54)
Proof.

Let mit=maxai∈𝒜it⁡Qit​(ai)m_{i}^{t}=\max_{a_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{i}^{t}}Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i}), which exists because 𝒜it\mathcal{A}_{i}^{t} is finite and nonempty. Since β^it≥0\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}\geq 0 by Equation 45, each summand of Equation 44 obeys β^it​Qit​(ai)≤β^it​mit\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i})\leq\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}m_{i}^{t}, hence

Qtott​(𝒞t,𝒂)≤bt+∑i∈ℐcommtβ^it​mitQ_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}(\mathcal{C}^{t},\bm{a})\;\leq\;b^{t}+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}m_{i}^{t} (55)

for every 𝒂∈𝒜t\bm{a}\in\mathcal{A}^{t}, and the bound is attained. Equality in Equation 55 holds if and only if Qit​(ai)=mitQ_{i}^{t}(a_{i})=m_{i}^{t}, that is ai∈ℳita_{i}\in\mathcal{M}_{i}^{t}, for every i∈𝒫ti\in\mathcal{P}^{t}, while for i∈𝒵ti\in\mathcal{Z}^{t} the term β^it​Qit​(ai)\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}Q_{i}^{t}(a_{i}) vanishes and the choice of aia_{i} leaves QtottQ_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t} unchanged. This establishes Equation 52, and ℳit⊆𝒜it\mathcal{M}_{i}^{t}\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{i}^{t} gives the subsequent claim. For the second part, finite logits make the softmax of Equation 43 strictly positive, so λi,ht>0\lambda_{i,h}^{t}>0 for all ii and hh. If Wt>0W^{t}>0 there exists a head h⋆h^{\star} with wh⋆t>0w_{h^{\star}}^{t}>0, whence β^it≥wh⋆t​λi,h⋆t>0\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}\geq w_{h^{\star}}^{t}\lambda_{i,h^{\star}}^{t}>0 for every eligible agent. Therefore 𝒵t=∅\mathcal{Z}^{t}=\varnothing and Equation 52 reduces to Equation 54. ∎

If all head weights vanish, then Qtott=btQ_{\mathrm{tot}}^{t}=b^{t} for every candidate joint action; independently greedy actions remain joint maximizers by Equation 52, but the two maximizing sets need not coincide. The condition Wt>0W^{t}>0 of Equation 53 can be enforced through a strictly positive head-weight parameterization whenever the set-valued identity is required.

Remark C.9 (Reachable coefficients and the cost of monotonicity).

Because λ⋅,ht\lambda_{\cdot,h}^{t} is normalized over ℐcommt\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}, the learned coefficients satisfy

∑i∈ℐcommtβ^it=∑h=1Hwht​∑i∈ℐcommtλi,ht=Wt.\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}=\sum_{h=1}^{H}w_{h}^{t}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}\lambda_{i,h}^{t}=W^{t}. (56)

The mixer therefore redistributes a single state-dependent mass WtW^{t} across agents rather than rescaling each utility independently, and by Equation 50 it cannot represent the negative sensitivities that Equation 41 permits. Both restrictions are the price of monotonicity, which is what makes Equation 54 and hence decentralized greedy execution available (Rashid et al., 2018). What β^it\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t} adds relative to a state-only mixer is not expressiveness in the utilities but the dependence of the normalized credit profile on 𝒩iin,t\mathcal{N}_{i}^{\mathrm{in},t} and 𝒩iout,t\mathcal{N}_{i}^{\mathrm{out},t} established in Corollary C.4; the empirical claim of this paper is that this monotonic, topology-conditioned class suffices for the communication action space of Section 3.2, not that it is universal.

Remark C.10 (Scope of the consistency result).

Theorem C.8 relies on the temporal ordering of Eqs. equation 29–equation 30: all candidate actions at round tt share one pre-decision context and therefore one set of mixing coefficients, and the selected action determines only the next topology. Without this ordering—for instance if the mixer were conditioned on the topology induced by the candidate action itself—the coefficients would vary across 𝒜t\mathcal{A}^{t}, the decomposition in Equation 44 would no longer be a fixed weighted sum, and monotonicity in each QitQ_{i}^{t} would not imply Equation 54.

Appendix D ACTS Training and Decentralized Execution

We reuse the GNN–GRU encoder and relational-attention/QQ branch of Section 3.2 and the topology encoder and topological mixer of Section 3.3. For Gt=(ℐ,ℰt)G^{t}=(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{E}^{t}), write 𝒩iin,t={j∣(j,i)∈ℰt}\mathcal{N}_{i}^{\mathrm{in},t}=\{j\mid(j,i)\in\mathcal{E}^{t}\} and 𝒩iout,t={j∣(i,j)∈ℰt}\mathcal{N}_{i}^{\mathrm{out},t}=\{j\mid(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}^{t}\} for the directed neighborhoods encoded by zitz_{i}^{t} in  equation 9. The operator BuildTopology denotes the topology construction map defined in Appendix B. The six actions are listed in Appendix E.3, and the observation and state vectors are specified in Appendix E.2. The action aoffa^{\mathrm{off}} suppresses both backbone inference and communication. The action asoloa^{\mathrm{solo}} invokes one independent backbone inference without creating communication edges, and its output is retained for final answer aggregation. The corresponding agent is excluded from subsequent communication rounds. All other actions produce an output and induce communication edges according to the selected mode. These messages enter the observations of round t+1t+1.

Every round is organized around the pre-decision context 𝒞t=(st,Gt,ℐcommt,{ξit,zit}i∈ℐcommt)\mathcal{C}^{t}=(s^{t},G^{t},\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t},\{\xi_{i}^{t},z_{i}^{t}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}}), computed from the realized topology before any action is selected and held fixed while candidate actions are compared, so the coefficients β^it=∑hwht​λi,ht\widehat{\beta}_{i}^{t}=\sum_{h}w_{h}^{t}\lambda_{i,h}^{t} are constants of 𝒞t\mathcal{C}^{t} and  equation 12 applies. Since agents outside ℐcommt\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t} are assigned aoffa^{\mathrm{off}},  equation 1 gives ℐcommt+1⊆ℐcommt\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t+1}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{comm}}^{t}. An agent selecting aoffa^{\mathrm{off}} or asoloa^{\mathrm{solo}} therefore withdraws from subsequent communication, although only aoffa^{\mathrm{off}} suppresses the current-round backbone inference. Hard partner-set construction is nondifferentiable, so relational attention is supervised only through the soft feature ξit\xi_{i}^{t} while topological attention is trained through the mixer; the target branch is detached, and replay stores raw inputs and topologies rather than cached hidden states.

Appendix E Experimental Details

E.1 Training and Evaluation Details

Benchmarks and backbone models.

We evaluate ACTS on nine benchmarks across four domains. The coding benchmarks are LiveCodeBench v6 and HumanEval (Jain et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2021). The reasoning benchmarks are MMLU-Pro and the first 250 questions of Humanity’s Last Exam (Wang et al., 2024; Phan et al., 2025). HotpotQA is used for multi-hop question answering (Yang et al., 2018). The mathematical benchmarks are AIME 2025, AIME 2026, HMMT 2025, and Beyond-AIME (Mathematical Association of America, 2025; Mathematical Association of America, 2026; MathArena, 2025; ByteDance-Seed, 2025). Each AIME benchmark comprises 30 problems from the corresponding AIME I and AIME II examinations. Experiments use GPT-OSS-120B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash as frozen backbone LLMs. Experiments use GPT-OSS-120B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash as frozen backbone LLMs. Each task is instantiated with three role-conditioned agents followed by a final answer-aggregation node.

Baselines and controlled comparison.

We compare ACTS with direct prompting, LLM-Debate (Du et al., 2023), AutoGen (Wu et al., 2023), LangGraph (LangChain AI, 2024), Microsoft Agent Framework (Microsoft, 2025), TopoDIM (Sun et al., 2026), and Agent Q-Mix (Jiang et al., 2026). All methods use the same team size (N=3N=3), task prompts, communication-round budget, and answer-evaluation procedure.

Training protocol and evaluation.

The ACTS scheduler is trained for 50 episodes using 15 training examples per domain. The communication budget is three rounds for mathematical tasks and two rounds for coding and reasoning tasks. All trainable modules are optimized with Adam using learning rate 5×10−45\times 10^{-4} and discount factor γ=0.99\gamma=0.99. The replay buffer has capacity 5,0005{,}000, the minibatch size is 88, and ϵ\epsilon-greedy exploration is annealed linearly from 1.01.0 to 0.050.05 over 50 episodes. The learned parameters are fixed during evaluation. Reported results are averaged over three independent runs with different random seeds.

E.1.1 Data Sampling and Information Gain Computation

For each model MM, benchmark DD, and topology family CC, empirical communication gain is defined as Δ⁡(M,D,C)=meanm∈C⁡ACC⁡(m,M,D)−ACC⁡(Direct,M,D)\Delta(M,D,C)=\operatorname{mean}_{m\in C}\operatorname{ACC}(m,M,D)-\operatorname{ACC}(\mathrm{Direct},M,D), with accuracy expressed as a fraction. The threshold x=2/nx=2/n is a heuristic tolerance corresponding to two correct answers among nn evaluation samples. A positive gain is identified when at least one topology family satisfies Δ⁡(M,D,C)>x\Delta(M,D,C)>x. Otherwise, no positive gain is identified under this criterion. This descriptive threshold does not establish statistical significance.

E.2 States and Observations

ACTS follows a centralised-training, decentralised-execution scheme. A shared per-agent value network receives a local observation oio_{i} for each agent ii, while a mixing network integrates the agent-specific values into a joint estimate QtotQ_{\mathrm{tot}} conditioned on a global state ss. We describe the construction of each.

Local observation.

For N=3N=3, each agent receives a 51-dimensional observation oito_{i}^{t} comprising a 32-dimensional task embedding, a 16-dimensional one-hot agent identifier, a binary indicator of whether the agent has produced an answer, its incident edge count, and the normalized cumulative team token consumption clipped to [0,1][0,1].

Global state.

The global state sts^{t} concatenates all agents’ local observations, three topology statistics comprising the edge count, graph density, and agent count, and the flattened N×NN\times N relational-attention matrix. For N=3N=3, the resulting state dimension is 3×51+3+9=1653\times 51+3+9=165.

E.3 Action Space

At each round every active agent selects one of six discrete actions, grouped into three roles. Three actions, off, solo, and broadcast, operate outside the attention matrix: off deactivates the agent entirely for the round, emitting no edges and issuing no LLM call, and once a majority of agents are inactive the episode terminates early; solo produces an independent answer and emits no edges; broadcast sends the agent’s current output to every other agent. Two actions build sparse directed edges from the learned attention matrix aedgea_{\mathrm{edge}}: attn-broadcast opens an edge i→ji\!\to\!j when the attention that agent jj pays to ii exceeds the row mean, and attn-receive requests information only from the neighbours that agent ii itself attends to. The remaining action, receive, performs a generic information fetch. Figure 7 reports the learned distribution of these six actions across the nine benchmarks.

E.4 Case Study

Figure 8 illustrates the same machinery at the trajectory level on one HotpotQA question and one HLE question. On HotpotQA the agents remain active throughout: several agents take the broadcast action, sending their analysis of the question to the team while one agent retains the solo action as an independent reference, after which the broadcasting agents switch to attn-receive, so that the initially connected topology contracts into a sparse pull while the informative edges are preserved. On HLE one agent settles the answer under the solo action, a single attn-broadcast check is routed only to the agent that requires it, and the remaining agents are successively deactivated through the off action, with the majority-inactive condition terminating the episode early. The two trajectories correspond to the two mechanisms that the aggregate action shares in Figure 6 average over: selective routing when the agents contribute complementary information, and deactivation when a single perspective suffices.

E.5 Per-Sample Token Usage

Table 4 lists the average per-sample token consumption of each method on HotpotQA, a high-information-gain (IG>0\mathrm{IG}>0) task, and HLE, a low-information-gain (IG≈0\mathrm{IG}\approx 0) task, for both backbone models. These are the numbers plotted against accuracy in Figure 4. Single-agent prompting uses the fewest tokens in every column, but at the cost of substantially lower accuracy; ACTS consumes the fewest tokens among all multi-agent methods in every column, while the static topologies are the most expensive because they broadcast the full running transcript to every agent each round.

E.6 Agent Role Assignments and Prompts

Each agent in the multi-agent system is assigned one of six predefined roles. Roles are allocated in round-robin fashion by agent index modulo 6. Since our experiments use n=3n=3 agents, only the first three roles are instantiated in any given run:

  1. R1:

    Independent Solver — solves the problem autonomously without relying on peer input.

  2. R2:

    Team Solver — approaches the problem collaboratively, integrating suggestions from teammates.

  3. R3:

    Questioner — probes assumptions and raises critical questions about the problem.

The remaining three roles (Refiner, Verifier, Debater) are defined in the role pool for future extensibility to larger agent teams, or for experiments where n>3n>3 (e.g., n=6n=6). The round-robin allocation modulo 6 naturally activates them when the team size increases, without any change to the prompt construction logic.

E.6.1 Agent System Prompt

Every agent receives a system prompt that instantiates its role within an nn-agent team and instructs it on the expected output format. The general template is:

You are {ROLE} on a {nn}-agent team. {SUFFIX}

where {ROLE} is one of the six role labels listed above and {SUFFIX} is a question-type-specific instruction detailed below.

E.6.2 Question-Type Suffixes

The suffix appended to each agent’s system prompt depends on the answer_type of the question. Five answer types are supported:

numerical.

“Solve the problem step by step, then state the final numerical answer. End with a line ‘Final Answer: <number>’.”

multiple_choice.

“This is a single-choice question; there is exactly one correct option. The options may be labeled with any letter from A up to Z (not just A–E), so read all options carefully before choosing. Briefly analyze why each candidate is right or wrong, then commit to exactly one option. End with a line ‘Final Answer: <letter>’ (e.g., ‘Final Answer: G’).”

text.

“Answer concisely. If a number, give the number. If a name, give the name. End with a line ‘Final Answer: <answer>’.”

open_answer.

“Answer concisely in a few words. End with a line ‘Final Answer: <answer>’.”

code.

“Write the complete, runnable solution code. Output ONLY the code—no markdown fences, no explanation.”

E.6.3 User Message

The user message delivered to each agent is constructed by concatenating the following components in order:

  1. 1.

    The question text.

  2. 2.

    Answer options (only for multiple_choice questions), formatted as A. ..., B. ..., etc.

  3. 3.

    Reference passages, when provided by the dataset (e.g., supporting documents for multi-hop QA).

  4. 4.

    Previously generated answers from inbound neighbors in the communication topology, listed as Agent {i}: {answer}.

E.6.4 Final Decision Maker

After all agents have executed across all rounds, a Final Decision Maker reviews the collected answers and produces the single final output. Its system prompt is:

You are the Final Decision Maker of a {nn}-agent team. Read the task and all agents’ answers carefully, then give the correct single answer.

The corresponding user message includes the original question, options (if applicable), reference context, and the full list of agent answers, followed by the instruction Give the final answer.

E.6.5 No-Role Baseline

For ablation experiments, we also evaluate a variant where all agents share an identical, role-agnostic system prompt:

You are a general team member on a {nn}-agent team. {SUFFIX}

This removes the role specialization signal while keeping all other aspects of the prompt (question-type suffix, user message structure, and communication topology) unchanged.
